title: Real GDP growth by state: Second quarter 2026
gist: BEA's Q2 2026 state GDP data show 44 of 50 states plus DC growing and 2.2% national growth, but the median state (Iowa) grew only 1.7% and 32 states lagged the national rate. Finance-led New York (4%) and Delaware topped the list while mining-hit West Virginia (-2.3%) and Wyoming (-1.6%) contracted; Q1 revisions averaged about +/- 2 points, underscoring how unreliable first prints are.

insights.claim: In Q2 2026, 44 of 50 US states plus Washington, DC posted positive real GDP growth, with the national average at 2.2% annualized (BEA data released September 30, 2026).
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Expansion remained broad-based in Q2 2026; no sign of a synchronized state-level downturn.
insights.quote: 44 of 50 state economies plus Washington, DC, grew in the second quarter. The national average was at 2.2% annualized growth.

insights.claim: The median US state (Iowa) grew only 1.7% annualized in Q2 2026, below the 2.2% national average, and 32 states grew slower than the national rate.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Headline GDP is skewed by a few large, fast-growing states; the typical state economy is closer to ~1.7% growth.
insights.quote: The median state, Iowa, grew at 1.7%, which is below the national average. 32 states had slower growth than the national average.

insights.claim: The gap between the median state's growth (1.7%) and national growth (2.2%) implies US Q2 2026 output gains were concentrated in a minority of large economies such as New York.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Regional-exposed assets (regional banks, munis, local consumer plays) may see weaker conditions than national GDP suggests.

insights.claim: New York had the fastest annualized real GDP growth of any state in Q2 2026 at 4%, followed by South Carolina and Delaware at 3.5%.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.quote: New York had the fastest annualized growth, at 4%. South Carolina and Delaware were next, at 3.5% growth.

insights.claim: Per the BEA, finance and insurance were the leading contributors to Q2 2026 real GDP growth in New York and Delaware.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Strong financial-sector activity (markets, deal flow) is a material driver of headline US GDP in Q2 2026.
insights.quote: finance and insurance sectors were the leading contributors to the increase in real GDP in New York and Delaware
insights.locator: According to the BEA press release

themes.theme: Laggards: mining and energy states contract

insights.claim: Six states contracted in Q2 2026: Alaska, Kansas, Nebraska, North Dakota, West Virginia, and Wyoming, with West Virginia steepest at -2.3% and Wyoming at -1.6%.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Contraction is clustered in resource- and farm-heavy states.
insights.quote: West Virginia had the steepest contraction, at -2.3%, followed by Wyoming, at -1.6%.

insights.claim: Per the BEA, mining was the leading contributor to the Q2 2026 real GDP declines in West Virginia and Wyoming.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Weak extractive output (coal, oil, gas) is dragging commodity-state economies; watch energy/mining activity indicators.
insights.quote: Mining was the leading contributor to the decline in West Virginia and Wyoming.
insights.locator: According to the BEA press release

insights.claim: The set of contracting states in Q2 2026 (energy/mining and agricultural states like North Dakota, Wyoming, Kansas, Nebraska, Alaska) points to a commodity-sector soft patch while finance-heavy states outperformed.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A finance-vs-commodity divergence in the real economy is consistent with weak energy/ag prices or volumes in Q2 2026.

insights.claim: All eight states in the St. Louis Fed's Eighth District grew in Q2 2026 but every one grew slower than the 2.2% national average; Mississippi and Illinois were fastest at 2.1%.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: The Midwest/Mid-South region is lagging national growth, relevant for regional Fed commentary.
insights.quote: with all eight growing slower than the national average. Mississippi and Illinois grew the fastest, at 2.1%.
insights.locator: The St. Louis Fed’s Eighth District

insights.claim: Q1 2026 state GDP growth rates were revised by an average of about +/- 2 percentage points across all states and DC, making first-print state data highly unreliable.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Treat initial state GDP prints with wide error bands; avoid trading regional narratives on first estimates.

insights.claim: Alaska's Q1 2026 growth was revised down from 2.8% to -3.8%, the largest downward revision, while Washington, DC was revised up from 2.2% to 7.3%, the largest upward revision.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Revisions can flip the sign of growth, so state-level recession calls from initial data are fragile.
insights.quote: The largest downward revision was for Alaska: from 2.8% to -3.8%.

insights.claim: State GDP data are subject to revision with an annual revision the following March, and FRED's ALFRED database preserves data vintages so users can see what was known at each point in time.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Use ALFRED vintages for backtests to avoid look-ahead bias from revised state data.
insights.quote: Our ALFRED database records vintages of the data, so users can view the data as they appeared at various points in history.
